correctness.rationale: Start from D and ignore jumps that stay in D: the waiting time to either absorption or S is Exp(2m/d), with absorption probability 1/m at that event. The rate to S is 2(m−1)/d. From S the next event is Exp(2) and leads to D. These relations do not depend on the actual vertices and give almost-sure absorption by geometric renewal. With F_X the transform, F_S=2F_D/(s+2) and F_D=[2/d+2(m−1)F_S/d]/[s+2m/d]. Hence the stated numerator and denominator d s²+2Ns+4 follow. Log derivatives at zero give mean N/2 and variance N²/4−d/2 for S; log((s+2)/2) subtracts 1/2 from the mean and 1/4 from the variance for D. The distinct positive rates follow from (N−2)²+4(m−1)>0. S is a sum of the two exponentials; with Δ=λ_+−λ_- its hazard is λ_-(1−exp(−Δt))/(1−(λ_-/λ_+)exp(−Δt)), strictly increasing to λ_-. In D, the monic rate polynomial at 2/d is 4(1−m)/d², so for m>1 the initial hazard 2/d lies strictly between the two rates and the asserted mixture weights are positive. Its hazard derivative is minus the variance of the rate under the time-t survivor weights. With m=1, S is unavailable and D has constant rate 2/(N−1). At fixed N comparisons are among admissible divisors/part sizes, and conditional, not over a mixture of initial classes. value.rationale: The object is the standard encounter law on a canonical family with two intrinsic starting relations. The precise comparison shows when common means lose the geometry, recovers part size from conditional variance, and finds opposite effects of conditioning on survival as time passes. This is more than rewriting a generic resolvent or giving an isolated variance: it classifies the law and hazard across an infinite family and distinguishes starting classes for modelling encounters.
